cross_exam_prompt_render.why: harness-log: CROSS_EXAM_PROMPT contains a JSON output template, so str.format() treats its { } as placeholders and raises KeyError. Rendering was extracted into build_cross_exam_message() and must keep using str.replace().

mutations.desc: Re-inject the original defect: render with str.format(colleagues=...) instead of str.replace().
Inline the rendering back into cross_examine(), leaving build_cross_exam_message() as dead code. The behavioural tests stay green; only the structural test can catch this divergence.

stdout_gbk_guard.why: P4: when stdout is redirected, Python falls back to the local code page (GBK / cp936), so printing a character GBK cannot encode raises UnicodeEncodeError and throws away the whole output plus the exit code. The correct guard -- measured, not reasoned -- is reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="replace"); both keywords are required.

mutations.desc: Guard sys.stderr instead of sys.stdout: the guard is textually present and looks right, but stdout still crashes.

Drop encoding="utf-8", keeping only errors="replace". Nothing crashes any more, but the output stays GBK bytes and is unreadable to anything that reads UTF-8. This is exactly the mistake the author made first.
Call reconfigure(encoding="utf-8", errors="strict"): strict IS the default, so the error mode is exactly equivalent to having no guard at all -- yet it looks identical to the real thing.

chat_call_signature.why: A call site passed max_tokens=2048 to DeepSeekClient.chat(), whose signature has no such parameter. No unit test could reach it (the adjudication step costs real API calls), so it only exploded after the whole multi-agent loop had run and the money was already spent. The seal is a static check that every chat() call site matches the real signature.

mutations.desc: Re-inject the historical defect: pass max_tokens=2048 to chat() inside adjudicate().

scoring_and_reproducibility.why: Three separate ways the D7 measurement lied: (#16) the keyword scorer counted a mention that the answer explicitly DISMISSED, so the multi-agent run was scored 100% while it had actually fallen for the red herring; (#17) the cross-examination step budget was hardcoded to 4 and not wired to --max-steps, while the report told the user to raise --max-steps; (#18) CrossExam snapshots omitted `finished`, so a 'convergence 0%' report could not say which role failed; (#19) root_cause was truncated to 400 chars while `correct` was computed on the full text, so 2 of 18 stored verdicts could not be reproduced from their own archive.

mutations.desc: #16: remove the dismissal check, so a keyword counts even when the answer explicitly rejects it. This is exactly how the red-herring verdict was scored 100%.

#17: give cross_examine a default step budget again (4, as it was). A default lets a caller spend a budget nobody measured without deciding anything.

fault_catalog_integrity.why: A fault definition carries two hand-written lists: `patches` (what really changes) and `changes` (what gets written to the change log). Their only link is an env-var name, so a mismatch is silent: the scenario still runs and still writes data, but the change record comes out as `from: null, to: null`. That is corrupted data, not a harder scenario -- and it only shows up when a NEW fault is added, which is exactly when nobody is looking.

mutations.desc: Restore the historical bug: map env-var names through a short hand-maintained dict with an env_key.lower() fallback. Then any newly added fault silently writes null change values.
Drop the pool_size -> pool_limit alias, so F2's change key stops resolving. Shows the self-check covers aliased names too, not just derived ones.

#20: make the F7 precondition guard a no-op. F7's whole value is that the recorded change is causally irrelevant, which only holds while concurrency < pool capacity. A guard that no longer guards turns F7 back into F2's mistake.

invalidated_scenario_exclusion.why: #20: F2's ground truth was proven inverted by a control experiment, but the scenario is kept in the catalog as a documented counter-example. That creates a new risk -- the bad question keeps polluting every accuracy comparison, invisibly (you just think 'accuracy is low'). Excluding it must be a mechanism (a field + filtering in the aggregate + disclosure in the report), not a matter of remembering.

mutations.desc: Stop filtering invalidated scenarios out of the aggregate -- the historical behaviour, where a wrong question silently drags every number down.
mutations.find: scored = [a for a in self.attempts if a.fault_id not in invalidated]

mutations.desc: Keep excluding invalidated scenarios but stop reporting them. Then the reader believes every scenario was counted -- 'the number looks fine, but it is not measuring what you think'.

two_axis_cause_scoring.why: F8 exposed a third outcome that a single keyword judgement cannot express: 'a specialist FOUND it, but the adjudication demoted it'. Scoring that as correct reproduces #21's false positive; scoring it as a plain miss conflates it with baseline's 'never found it at all'. The fix splits the judgement into a verdict axis (did the final answer assert it) and a recall axis (did any component find it).

mutations.desc: Make the recall axis look only at the final answer, ignoring the specialists' claims. Then multi's only real advantage -- the division of labour covering the second fault -- becomes invisible, and the two systems look identical.

Score a required cause by plain substring matching, ignoring dismissal context. The demoted leak in the F8 verdict then counts as asserted -- the #21 false positive, reintroduced through the new two-axis path.

loop_defense_and_static_guard.why: D9. Two findings. (#24) Measured evidence: one baseline attempt made 87 tool calls in 14 steps and produced nothing -- and the report could not tell 'digging deeper' from 'spinning in place', which need opposite fixes. Detection lives in ToolBox.call, the single exit for tool calls, so every agent gets it. (#23) Three times an edit swallowed a function's `def` line, leaving its body absorbed into the previous function -- which is VALID Python, so ast.parse stays silent and the loss only shows up as a runtime NameError.

mutations.desc: Raise the warning threshold so the model is never told it is repeating itself. Counting without telling is useless -- the model cannot see the counter and just keeps going.

Compare the raw argument string instead of the normalised arguments. Re-asking the same question with different spacing or key order then looks like new evidence, so spinning gets recorded as broadening the search.

Put the 'what have I already asked' state on the ToolBox instead of the RunContext. Then a second box over the same context silently resets detection while repeat_calls stays 0 -- looking exactly like 'no looping'. A plausible refactor (moving `box = ToolBox(ctx)` into the loop) triggers this.
Drop the looping branch from stop_reason, so 'spinning in place' is reported as a plain budget overrun. The two need opposite fixes: raise the budget vs change the prompt.

seal_checklist_integrity.why: The sealing checklist reconciles two things that can drift apart: the human claim written in docs/harness-log.md, and whether the mutation actually turns the tests red. If its parser silently reads nothing from the table, the reconciliation becomes vacuously green -- 'no declarations found, so everything is consistent'. That is precisely the failure mode the checklist exists to prevent, so the parser itself needs a proved mutation.

mutations.desc: Make the status parser read an empty document. Every declared sealing claim becomes invisible -- and, crucially, the gate ('no unbacked claims') would then pass VACUOUSLY, because an empty declaration map trivially has nothing unbacked. This is why that gate also asserts how many declarations it read.

historical_world_integration_only.why: These three were sealed only by Docker integration tests, which a copy-mutation harness fundamentally cannot validate: the tests hit the RUNNING containers, and the containers run the real source, not the mutant copy. So offline structural guards were added for the invariants they protect -- not replacing the end-to-end evidence, but making the fix continuously checkable offline and mutation-provable.

mutations.desc: #5: shrink the default stock back to 1000. A scenario fires thousands of requests, so stock runs out, requests short-circuit with 409 and payment goes quiet -- which then LOOKS like 'the fault injection had no effect'.

#7: remove the worker-side request cap and rely on the monitor loop that wakes every 5 seconds. It then overshoots the target by more than 50% (1200 requested, 1841 sent), and the data volume stops being reproducible.
#8: inject only the retry amplification, with a healthy payment. Retries only fire on failure, so nothing ever fires -- the scenario produced zero 5xx and was indistinguishable from the baseline.

json_contract_repair.why: #27: the JSON parse rate fell from 100% to 67% after the task changed, and on a parse failure the code scored the model's RAW text -- which mixes its reasoning with its conclusion. That silently loosened the measurement ('mentioned a word while thinking' is not 'asserted it in the conclusion', the root of the #16/#21 false positives). The fix is a one-shot nudge to re-emit JSON, shared by all three call sites.

mutations.desc: Remove the nudge call site from baseline, so a non-JSON answer is accepted as-is and scored on raw reasoning text. The shared-logic check must catch this.

Make the repair REPLACE the conversation instead of appending to it. The model then loses every piece of evidence it had gathered and must start over -- the nudge would do more harm than the bad format.

keyword_verdict_conjunction.why: #28: the keyword side's three-way verdict decided 'was it mentioned at all' with ANY-group matching, while a cause's criterion is ALL-groups (a conjunction). So an answer that never mentioned the retry config counted as 'mentioned but denied' merely because its propagation chain contained the word 'inventory'. Silent -- it only distorted the agreement numbers used to compare two rulers.

mutations.desc: Revert to ANY-group matching for 'was it mentioned'. An answer that only touches one group of a conjunction criterion is then misread as 'mentioned but dismissed' instead of 'absent'.
